Indian Act

The house resumed from Tuesday, February 14, consideration in committee of Bill No. 21, to amend the Indian Act.-Mr. Murphy- Mr. Sullivan in the chair.
Section 6 agreed to.
On section 7-Inquiry as to fitness for enfranchisement.
Might I ask the minister to explain.

Section 110 as it exists in the act at the present time, the hon. member will find printed on the right hand page of the proposed bill. The proposed amendment reads:
The Superintendent General may appoint a board to consist of two officers of the department and a member of the band to which the Indian or Indians under investigation belong, to make inquiry and report as to the fitness of any Indian or Indians too be enfranchised.
You will observe that the act as at present in force reads that the Indian may be enfranchised upon the application of himself or of a band on a vote of a majority of the male members of such band of the full age of twenty-one years at a meeting or council thereof summoned for that purpose. Under the amended section the Superintendent General would be given the power to appoint a board to consist of two officers of the department and a member of the band to which the Indian or Indians under investigation belong, to make inquiry and report as to the fitness of any Indian or Indians to be enfranchised.
Will the minister inform me how many have been enfranchised under the old section 110?

During the ten year
period from 31st December, 1922, to the 31st December, 1932, under section 122a of the old act and section 114 of the new, 793 Indians were enfranchised.
Under section 107 of the old act and 110 of the new-that is the act which is at present in force-61 Indians were enfranchised during the same period.
I may say that the majority of the Indians enfranchised during the past few years have been enfranchised under section 114 of the present act rather than section 110. Under section 114 Indians are enfranchised who live and make their living away from the reserve. Section 110 refers more to the enfranchisement of Indians living on the reserve.
Will the minister give the total number of Indians enfranchised in the dominion?

The figures I have given
for the ten year period comprise all those enfranchised during those years. When an Indian is enfranchised his wife and minor children are enfranchised automatically. If he has children over the age of twenty-one it is necessary for them to be enfranchised of themselves.

I understand under the electoral act, at least as far as northern Ontario is concerned, only Indians who are war veterans have the right to vote. I believe the law should be uniform throughout Canada for all Indians. I have in mind that during the last general election a party organizer for one of the great parties in Canada sent a letter to one of the candidates to the effect that a certain number of Indians should vote because they were good Conservatives. He was certain of that. We want to do away with that. I do not believe that any man in Canada should say who has a right to vote and who has not. That right is vested in this parliament, and we should have a uniform law that applies to the whole of Canada. I know this anomaly has existed in my section of the country and also in other sections. I protest as strenuously as I can against such a measure. I believe that under the electoral act only Indians who enlisted during the great war have a right to vote. Under this act it is going to be left to one or two men to decide what Indians shall have that right. I protest against that. Either it should be general, that an Indian has the right to vote no matter where he lives, or else no Indian should be allowed to vote. I speak feelingly in this matter, because I know the electoral act is not properly applied, in my section of the country at least, and this would only create another gap which will allow some men, perhaps competent men, in most cases honest men, but in some cases subject to political influence, to pick out certain people to whom the right to vote would be given, and keep it from others. I say this law should be uniform for all Indians. No body of men in Canada, no matter how able they may be, should be given the power to say whether or not an Indian is entitled to vote. We know what happened at the last general election, and so far as I am concerned I do not want the same thing to happen again.

As I understood my hon. friend, he was making some complaint with regard to the voting system. This section merely provides for the enfranchisement of the Indians, and not for the actual voting.
Indian Act

It would appear to me that the amendment suggested by my hon. friend, which I could not hear distinctly, has reference to the electoral act rather than to the Indian Act, which only provides for enfranchisement.

I believe the two questions of enfranchisement and voting cannot be separated. What I had in mind was this: Under the present electoral act and the Indian Act, even at the last general election certain men were allowed to say whether or not certain Indians should vote. That is why I am protesting now. Once the Indians become enfranchised under this act they have the right to vote; if they have not the franchise they have not the right to vote. I maintain that the law should be uniform with regard to the Indians, as it is for the white men. Under this statute there will be no uniformity for the simple reason that you leave it to two or three men to decide what Indians shall vote. They may be quite competent men, but certainly they should not have the right to give the franchise to certain people only. That right is vested in this parliament, and I am afraid that the same things that took place during previous elections will happen again under this amendment. I think there should be a uniform law applying to all the Indians throughout Canada, and I do not believe any body of men should be given power to pick out certain Indians who may become enfranchised and have the right to vote.
I make this protest very sincerely for the sake of the good name of our elections. People should know exactly wrhere they stand. If the minister would like me to do so I could give him some correspondence that came into my hands accidentally. In the town of Mattice, near Hearst, which the Minister of Labour knows quite well, a certain number of Indians spend the summer months. During the last general election I came into possession of a certain letter giving information to my opponent. I do not know who wrote the letter, whether or not it was the agent of the department, but this letter singled out a certain number of Indians who should be allowed to vote because they were good Conservatives and a certain number of Indians who should not be allowed to vote because they were good Grits. I want to see these uncertainties done away with, but I believe we will only continue that system by this amendment. I believe each Indian should know exactly where he stands when an election comes along, and I repeat that you cannot separate the franchise and the right to vote. I appeal

to the sense of justice of the minister and the government; I ask them to bring in a uniform law in this connection. This is the time and place to do it; it is only justice and British fair play to all concerned.
What qualifications fare necessary before an Indian can become enfranchised?

The general qualification would be the judgment of those who examine the Indian as to his fitness to be enfranchised. Frequently an Indian who does not live on a reserve applies of his own volition to be enfranchised. Upon receipt of the application reports are asked from the agent and other responsible people in the district as to the fitness of this particular Indian to be enfranchised, and after the reports are received and passed upon by the department a recommendation is made to the governor general in council. A number of Indians have been enfranchised in recent years; I gave the figures a moment ago. Practically fall these Indians came under section 114, which provides for the enfranchisement of those living off a reserve. Seotion 110, which we propose to amend, refers more particularly to those now residing or who may hereafter reside upon a reserve. I do not think I can make it any plainer than that.	.

For what purpose is the enfranchisement referred to in section 110? At what elections does it entitle the Indian to vote? Surely it does not refer to the right to vote at a dominion election, for instance?
It has nothing to do with the right to vote; it enfranchises the Indian and makes him a citizen of this country, with all the rights and privileges that go with citizenship.

Under the electoral act certain Indians only are entitled to vote at dominion elections. Do I understand the minister to mean that if the Indian is enfranchised, either under section 110 or section 114, he thereby becomes entitled to be added to the list that is already provided for under the Dominion Elections Act?
Yes.
May I ask the minister where the demand came from for this amendment? Did it come from the Indians on the reserves? Was it suggested by the department, or where did the suggestion come from?

Whatever merit there may be in the measure is not for me to say, but

Indian Act
the amendment originated with myself. The amendment before us was drafted within the department, by and with the advice of the officials.
Was there any demand from the Indians living on reserves to have this tribunal set up in this manner?
No.
Were the Indians consulted at all? _
A similar amendment was passed in 1920, when a committee of the house sat upon the matter and the Indians and all interested parties were represented.
Here in Ottawa?
Yes.
Were the Indians represented here at that time?
They appeared before the committee, yes.

I compliment the minister on this provision because for many years there has been a considerable demand from the Indians for enfranchisement, As I said the other day, there is no reason at all for fixing the colour line with respect to the right to vote. Must the Indian apply separately and specifically, or will the minister hold an investigation into his capability of exercising the franchise?

The proposed amendment
reads:
The Superintendent General may appoint a board to consist of two officers of the department and a member of the band, to which the Indian or Indians under investigation belongs, to make inquiry and report as to the fitness of any Indian or Indians to be enfranchised.
I would take it that a separate board would not be appointed for every indivdual Indian, although if an Indian made application, or it was decided to investigate his fitness, a board might be appointed for that purpose. But that same board could pass upon the fitness of more than one Indian at the time the sittings were held.

I do not think the minister caught my question. Would this board be competent to go into the band and examine all the Indians there, or will the individual have to make separate application to be enfranchised?

It would depend upon the instructions given the board. If the Superintendent General instructed the board to make a general investigation of the Indians of the band, it would be within the competence of the board to do so.

How does this affect the liability of the Indian for debt under the Indian Act? Suppose execution is recovered against the Indian; it does not become effective, so long as he remains a member of the band, as against any property on the reserve. Does this affect him when he becomes enfranchised? Does he then take all the rights and privileges of the ordinary citizen and lose the privilege that he formerly had of exemption from having his goods seized under execution?
After he became enfranchised he would certainly be in the same position as any other citizen of Canada.

Even if he lived on the
reserve?
Whether on or off the reserve, he has become enfranchised and is then subject to the laws of the country the same as an3' white man.

I understand that the franchise, the power to vote, is conferred in the first instance on Indians who served overseas in the Great war and, in the second place, there is enfranchisement through the procedure established in this act which is now being modified. As I understand the amendment at present before us, it is only to eliminate the initiative from the council of the band and to leave that initiative with the minister himself in relation to the board. Am I correct in my interpretation of the section?
Yes; it gives the Superintendent General the power to initiate the proceedings.

Without
consulting the band or the council?
The council must be consulted because they have the power to appoint one member of the board.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
As regards an Indian who continues to live on the reserve after enfranchisement, the land which he occupies is taken out of the reserve and becomes his private property, subject to taxation. He has all the civil rights of any other British subject and is similarly liable to be sued. Enfranchisement as understood in this act has no reference to the right to vote; it means
Indian Act

enfranchising the Indian in his right as a citizen. If any question as to the right to vote is raised, it will be more proper to raise it as an amendment to the election act than by way of amendment to the Indian Act.

I notice in the bill we are considering that the board of investigation is largely a departmental board. There are two representatives from the department to inquire into the fitness of any Indian to vote, and these representatives in many cases are thousands of miles away from the Indian reserve. If we are going to make this a real board competent to investigate the fitness of the Indian to vote, I submit that the head of the band should be on the board together with one man from the department and one representative selected from the community in which the reserve is situated. If that were done you would have a representative body of opinion on a question of great importance to the Indians.

The amendment provides that the Superintendent General may appoint a board to consist of two officers of the department. It does not necessarily follow that these two officers will be located in Ottawa. We have agents and inspectors throughout Canada and it would be quite competent for the Superintendent General to appoint an inspector and an agent, or two agents, as representatives of the department on the board.

That is a little better,
but it is more than likely that one of the men whom the department might appoint would reside, in the case of Saskatchewan, in Regina, and that is about as bad as if he were living in Ottawa. My point is this. If you appointed an Indian agent as a member of the board you would still be under a disadvantage in getting the considered community opinion regarding the fitness of the Indian to vote.

The members to be appointed could be the agent and inspector in that province, and the inspector is continually making his tours of the reserves in the province and is therefore quite familiar with the conditions as they exist. Furthermore, the boundaries of many of the reserves especially in the west are fairly close together, and two agents living side by side might constitute the board. When I say side by side I mean in contiguous territory. It would therefore be perfectly competent for them to pass upon the fitness of the Indian for enfranchisement, considering the case in conjunction with the Indian who is nominated by the council of the particular band.

This provision which
we are now considering proposes, as the minister has pointed out, that the Superintendent General may appoint a board to consist of two officers of the department and a member of the band to which the Indian belongs, to make inquiry and report as to his fitness to be enfranchised. What section of the act permits the Indian to make application for this body to investigate, or is that right vested in these officials, together with the Indian chosen from the band? Have they the right to pick out the Indian who is to be investigated?
An Indian on the reserve might himself desire enfranchisement and there is nothing to preclude his making application if he sees fit-

Suppose he did not
want to?
-in which case the board would act exactly in the same manner as it would if the Superintendent General were to direct an investigation to be made.

Is there any particular
section of the act that instructs the Indian to take such action?

The present section 110
which we are amending makes provision in that regard. We are only substituting this amendment for one subsection of section 110, which comprises thirteen subsections.

I would ask another
question prompted by the reply given by the Minister of Justice a few moments ago. I think I understood the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) to state that an Indian living on a reserve who applies for and obtains his enfranchisement would have his land taken out of the reserve and become a regular citizen of Canada.

Provided he has a
location upon the reserve.
And if he has not?

Subsection 8 of section
110 reads:
Upon the issue of an order of enfranchisement the Superintendent General shall, if any Indian enfranchised holds any land on a reserve, cause letters patent to be issued to such Indian for such land; and such Indian shall pay to the funds of the band such amount per acre for the land he holds as the Superintendent General considers to be the value of the common interest of the band in such land, and such payments shall be a charge against the share of such Indian in the funds of the band.

Indian Acl

Does that apply to
both treaty and non-treaty Indians, and would the Indian then be entitled to vote?
I would say that no distinction is made in the act between treaty and non-treaty Indians; it simply says "Indian."

The aot defines the
responsibilities of treaty and non-treaty Indians. I do not want to appear to be telling the minister something whioh he perhaps ought to know regarding his own department. I think there is a vast difference in what is expected by the state from a treaty and a non-treaty Indian. They are not in the same category; the one is a ward of the state while the other is not.

I cannot see any difference between section 110 as amended by this bill and the latter part of the original section. I should like to know why the first part of the section which provides for an Indian making application has been dropped?

Under the present act
there must be voluntary action by the Indian in making application while under the proposed amendment the initial proceedings might be started by the Superintendent General.

Is the minister in a
position to answer the questions I asked? I do not ask these in order to embarrass him.

Both the treaty and nontreaty Indian is mentioned in the act, but my opinion is that the term is used in this section in the generic sense and means all Indians. I do not think it is circumscribed in any way by the definition of a non-treaty Indian.

According to the interpretation given by the Minister of Justice, all we are dealing with is the treaty Indian living upon the reserve. When that Indian applies for enfranchisement and receives it he is no longer a treaty Indian entitled to the privileges of a ward. He cannot have both.
Quite so.
Under this bill you are permitting the treaty Indian to come out from under the treaty and assume all the responsibilities of citizenship?
Yes.

The note in connection with section 7 reads:
This subsection is designed to give the necessary impetus to carry out the ultimate aims and objects of the policy which has governed the administration of Indian affairs.
What impetus is being referred to?

Through the years the
Canadian people have recognized their responsibilities for the welfare of the Indians of this country. In furtherance of that recognition they have spent vast sums of money in order to raise the status of the Indian. In cooperation with the churches they have established a very comprehensive educational system comprising both residential and day schools. They have also provided medical and hospitalization services for the Indian and have spent large sums of money, notably in the west, in order to make the Indian self supporting upon our agricultural lands. This constant endeavour throughout the years to raise the status of the Indian has been for what purpose? What has been the ultimate object in view in the expenditure of these moneys and the providing of these services for the Indian? It has been to raise the Indian to full status where he can take his place as a citizen of Canada. I believe this policy is the correct one but so far we have failed to take that final step which, in my opinion, should be taken, namely, to make the Indian a full citizen of this country when he has obtained that degree of advancement which entitles him to the full responsibilities and privileges of citizenship.

Let us grant that what the minister has said is correct, but I want to point again to the proposed amendment as it compares with the original subsection. If I understand the minister aright he says that the real difference is that in the one case the action depended upon the volition of the Indian whereas under the proposed amendment this action may be taken by the department without consultation with the Indian. If I am correct in my interpretation, then I think it very essential that this distinction be drawn to the attention of the committee. Does the minister think that an Indian who has not had sufficient initiative to ask for enfranchisement is worthy of being enfranchised? Does he think that an Indian would be capable of exercising the rights of citizenship when he has not been willing to take the steps to attain that end? If this change is made the power will be given to departmental officials to enfranchise Indians at a
Indian Act

wholesale rate irrespective of the qualifications of the Indians and perhaps irrespective of their desire. At any rate, it would be apart altogether from their own volition.

It is urged that this
amendment is being made because the time has come when the Indian should be made a citizen. Is it not rather fathered by the thought of the $400, S500 or $600 band money for each Indian and is he not anxious to become enfranchised because at the expiration of two years 'he receives his franchise and gets this money; he is anxious to get it into his hands. Am I not correct in saying this is the reason for his wanting to become enfranchised?

I would say that the opposite is the case, because the Indians who are living on the reserves a*t this time have not over the years made application to become enfranchised although they would be entitled to their share in the funds of the band to which they belong. Applications that have been made for enfranchisement have generally been from those who are not living on the reserves, but who have gone out into the cities, towns and other localities and are there making their living in competition with the white man.

I am in absolute agreement with the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. McGibbon), when he says that we should give the Indians universal suffrage. I believe the Minister of Justice was answering the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario when he said that we were dealing with the electoral act. This measure is in conflict with the electoral act. We are going to take a certain portion of the population and decide, apart from the provisions of that act, whether they shall have the vote. In extending this franchise, we can extend it only to federal elections; we cannot give it for provincial or municipal elections, so that there again there will be a conflict with the municipalities and provinces. In my opinion, we should therefore leave aside this part of the act, the present section 110, because the Minister of Justice has said that in dealing with the matter we are dealing with the electoral act and it is not fair for any parliament to pass legislation picking out a certain section of the population and deciding whether they shall have the right to vote.
I agreed with the Minister of Justice when he said in answer -to the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario that so far as this parliament was concerned we could not give the

Indian universal suffrage except through the electoral act. I believe this section should be withdrawn now. Although I have no treaty Indians in my section, there are conflicts so far as the Indian vote is concerned. Some of -them do not know whether they have the right to vote or not. Whether the law is not well enough defined or not or universal enough is up to parliament to judge, but I believe if you create a body from the Indian department that will have power to extend the right to vote, you are going to cause still more conflict. We should let parliament decide the matter through the electoral act. From personal experience I belive it would be better either to enfranchise all Indians or to have all disenfranchised. The situation is confusing and even the chief electoral officer does not know in certain cases how to apply the act because it comes into conflict with the electoral act. I make this appeal very sincerely to the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think that what I have said has been misapprehended. This section we now propose to amend has been on the statute book for at least ten years and the amendment now proposed does not affect the right to use the electoral franchise one way or the other; we are not going to change the law in that respect. The only change that is proposed is as regards the manner in which an Indian shall apply for enfranchisement. Under the old section 110, subsection one, the Indian made the application. Now it is proposed by the amendment that the superintendent may make the application.
Why?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I thought that had been very well explained.
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
If it has not been, it will be. The other point that seems to have caused some trouble is whether it applied to all Indians. The section does apply to all Indians, treaty and non-treaty. My hon. friend will see that the section refers to an Indian and in the interpretation clause an Indian is defined:
1.	Any male person of Indian blood reputed to belong to a particular band.
2.	Any child of such person.
3.	Any woman who is or was lawfully married to such person.
A non-treaty Indian is also defined:	-
*'Non-treaty Indian" means any person of Indian blood who is reputed to belong to an irregular band, or who follows the Indian mode of life, even if such person is only a temporary resident in Canada.

Indian Act
Then an irregular band is described and defined:
*'Irregular band" means any tribe, band or body of persons of Indian blood who own no interest in any reserve or lands of which the legal title is vested in the crown, who possess no common fund managed by the government of Canada, and who have not had any treaty relations with the crown.
Section 110, as it has been upon the statute book for at least ten years, provides that any of these persons may under certain conditions become enfranchised. Enfranchisement confers upon them all the rights of a British subject; they may even buy and sell liquor. The right to the electoral franchise is only one of those rights. What I intended to convey in what I said before was that if this is meant to limit the right given, any amendment in that respect should be made to the Dominion Elections Aot and not to the Indian Act. I do not know that any amendment to the Dominion Elections Act is necessary, but such an amendment should certainly not be made to the Indian Act. This enfranchisement covers all the rights of a British subject.
Why is this change being made? It seems that its only effect is to take the responsibility away from the Indian and throw it into the hands of the officer.

A few moments ago I endeavoured to make plain the reason for the proposed amendment. There are in Canada to-day I would say a considerable number of Indians who have so far progressed that they should accept all the duties of citizenship.
Then let them ask for it.

My hon. friend says:
"Then let them ask for it." Let me point out, as has been done already, that under the Indian Act these people who are classed as Indians have certain rights and privileges, foT instance, in regard to their debts, as the hon. member for Laprairie-Napierville (Mr. Dupuis) indicated the other day. Recently in an indirect manner there came to my attention an instance where an Indian was carrying on a considerable manufacturing business in this country. He was assessed by the Department of Inland Revenue for the sum of 84,000 sales tax, which he paid. Later he secured the services of a legal firm who endeavoured to recover that amount of money from the department, on the ground that he was an Indian and carrying on his business on an Indian reserve. I leave it to the good sense of the committee to decide whether or not a man capable of carrying on business to the extent I have indicated,
namely to the point where he becomes liable for a 84,000 sales tax, should accept his responsibility as a Canadian citizen.
Was a judgment rendered?

I cannot say that, because I did not follow the case that far; in fact I am not certain as to whether or not a decision has been given. Further, may I point out that many Indians, so-called, have a greater proportion of white blood than Indian blood in their veins; yet they are still classed as Indians. Further, in some cases white children have been adopted by Indians and have become members of the band, thereby enjoying all the rights and privileges, if we wish to term them so, enjoyed by Indians. There might not be-and I believe, sometimes is not-one drop of Indian blood in their veins. Still they have all the privileges accorded to them under the Indian Aot.
Again, there are Indians of mixed blood who have left the reserves and gone to Montreal, Toronto or other Canadian cities and taken their places in the community in every respect, with the one exception that they do not exercise the right of voting. Possibly they cannot buy liquor legally. But for all other purposes they meet their white brothers on common ground, and compete with them. Then, there are many Indians to-day in Canada who belong to professions, and are as clever and brainy men as can be found anywhere. Is it reasonable that these people should not accept their full responsibility as citizens, rather than claim the privileges which are accorded to them because they have not seen fit to make application to become enfranchised.

I believe the minister
has succeeded in making clear the desire of the department. I take it from what he has said, and hope I am correct in my interpretation, that the department's desire to make the change by which it could enfranchise an Indian without receiving first a request to be enfranchised, as was provided under the old section, is because the department has found that certain Indians are evading their responsibilities as citizens, so far as their legal obligations are concerned. I should like to know whether it would be the intention of the department to go to a band which is not asking for enfranchisement, and enfranchise the Indians belonging to that band. Could the department take that action forcibly, and without first receiving a request from the Indians, in cases where there have been no violations of their rights as citizens?
Indian Act
I take it, Mr. Chairman, that any minister charged with the admin-tration of the department would have to make that decision, after considering all the circumstances.
To my mind that seems to be the important point.

But I would say that
before taking such action the minister responsible would have to consider all factors. For the information of the hon. member who has just spoken may I refer to subsection 3 of clause 110 which reads as follows:
In the course of such inquiry it shall be the duty of the board to take into consideration and report upon the attitude of any such Indian towards his enfranchisement which attitude shall be a factor in determining the question of fitness.
I do not anticipate it would be the desire of the department, or any responsible minister, to enforce enfranchisement against any great objection by a band of Indians.
But you could do it under the section?
Yes, it could be done.

I should like to sayand I believe the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario will agree with me-that the Indians themselves have a very strong desire for the franchise. On many occasions they have expressed their desire to candidates of both political parties. They urge that they are the first native Canadian citizens, and that the rest of us have descended from people who came to this country as foreigners. The Indians are the native Canadians. Regardless of the fact that the federal government has made a treaty with them to give them certain treaty moneys, and in that treaty have agreed that the Indians may fish and hunt so long as grass grows and water flows, and has agreed to give them ownership of certain lands- regardless of all that they believe they have the right to vote, and still receive the privileges under the treaty.
I believe the minister's point is well taken when he refers to Indians who leave reserves, who engage in business and try to avoid payment of taxes which might arise in the course of that business. I think the point is reasonably well taken that the department might say to him, "We maintain the right to state that you are a Canadian citizen and subject to the laws of Canada with regard to taxation." That ground may be well taken; but under the old act, as the minister so afely said, the Indians have always had the privilege of applying for citizenship. If their applications

are accepted they have to accept the obligations to which an ordinary citizen is subjected with regard to debts. The minister has pointed out that when they receive citizenship the land on the reserves which they have been holding is transferred to them in fee simple, they in turn incurring certain obligations to the band for the value of the land. The minute that becomes possible, the decision must be made whether the Indian can then sell the land to some white person who is not now on a reserve, or who may be objectionable to the other Indians at that point.
While the minister's point may be well taken, I do not think the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs or any other departmental official should have a right to go to a reserve and enforce enfranchisement of Indians who have not requested it, take away from them privileges they have enjoyed under the Indian Act, and place greater responsibilities upon them. I believe the position the Indians take-and I am referring to those bands in Ontario who are cultured, have good education and are farming intelligently, as obtains on some reserves with which I am familiar-that they have a right to vote at elections and still retain their Indian privileges, is a well founded claim. I submit suggestions made by the hon. member for North Timiskaming are well founded, and we would be wise to consider under the election act whether or not we might let the privilege of voting accrue to the Indians, without any reservation as to their civil rights.
I point out to the minister that, as every hon. member knows some of our Ontario bands sent practically every able bodied man to France. Of course those men were rewarded with the franchise, without incurring the responsibilities to which the minister has referred. How can we differentiate between the sons of those men who went overseas, and the fathers? They are the same type of Canadian citizens. Their fathers were enfranchised, and the boys who have now reached voting age cannot see why they should be deprived of that privilege. I place myself on record, with the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario, and the hon. member for North Timiskaming, in saying that we would be well advised to consider favourably giving to all the native Canadians who are called Indians the franchise for general elections.

I am afraid I will have to disagree with my good friend who has just spoken. Having had some experience in administering Indian affairs I see great difficulties that the minister would encounter if he tried to enfranchise the

Indian Act
Indians holus-bolus and leave them with the rights they possess under the Indian Act, because under that act they are wards of the government of Canada and possess a great many rights. Enfranchisement would give the Indian every right of a Canadian citizen, but then he could be no longer a ward of the government.

And at the same time
every responsibility.

Oh,
absolutely. He becomes a Canadian citizen in the fullest sense of the word. But as a ward of the government he can call upon the government for a great many privileges. For example the education of the Indians is pretty much the responsibility of the government. The Indian does not pay taxes, except such as he imposes on himself for the purposes of the reserve or the band. All these things have to be taken into consideration. Up to date enfranchisement has only taken place at the express desire of the Indian and with the consent of the band. All my hon. friend is attempting to do is to say he does not require that the Indian shall make application, but if he finds, after representation has been made, that any certain Indian would be better enfranchised for various reasons, which he has enumerated, then he does not have to go through the process provided under section 110. All he has to do is to appoint a board consisting of two officers of the department and a member of the band. I am not just clear if the minister stated that this member of the band would be the appointee of the council. If that is true then the council would have some say, but his amendment does not so state. That selection is made by himself, and those three decide whether or not a particular Indian is to be enfranchised. If they recommend his enfranchisement, undoubtedly it will take place. Where I see difficulty is in the adjustment that will have to take place between the individual Indian who is enfranchised and the band and band council, with respect to his property held in common with the rest of the band. Under section 110 as it existed that was all taken care of.
It is yet.

Then I do
not see it. I would be glad to have that explained.

We are not altering that
in the slightest. The same conditions will apply if he becomes enfranchised under this amendment.

Suppose the band refuse to act, what is going to happen? Suppose the band or the council of the band have not been consulted: a recommendation is made by the board that a particular Indian be enfranchised. If my hon. friend is correct and this third member of the board, the Indian member, is the nominee of the council, then it would be assumed that the council were consenting parties?
Yes.

But I do
not see that that is provided for in the section as drafted.

Yes, under subsection 2
of section 110, which reads as follows:
The Indian member of the board shall be nominated by the council of the band, within thirty days after the date of notice having been given to the council, and in default of such nomination, the appointment shall he made by the Superintendent General.

Are we then to come to this conclusion, that if a band of Indians do not want to avaiil themselves of subsection 7 of section 110 they are now going to be or may be forced by the department, to nominate this representative on the board, and if they do not nominate, then the department itself nominates an Indian whether he wants to sit or not?
That is the aot as at present in force, and as it has been for some ten years.

Yes, but the minister forgets that he is now giving power to this board to nominate someone who must come before themselves. That is what we object to. Coming as I do from the ancient seat of Battleford where there are many Indians, naturally I am interested in them, and I cannot conceive of an Indian suggesting to the minister, and I cannot see where the minister in his travels ever got the suggestion, that the Indians wanted to be forced into the position that he is trying to put them in. I have learned to-day that the Indian, when he becomes enfranchised, as a treaty Indian loses his treaty rights. What is to hinder the department from enfranchising all Indians and taking away their treaty and all the privileges they have, whether they like it or not?

I think any responsible minister charged with the administration of the Indian Aot, if he is a fit and proper person to administer the affairs of that department would never have such an idea in his mind as to force enfranchisement upon a body of Indians who were not fit for enfranchisement.

Indian Act

That is the thing we
are trying to prevent. Why should the minister be given that power?

For the reasons I endeavoured to give to the committee a few minutes ago, when I pointed out why this amendment is being asked for; simply because there are many Indians in Canada to-day who should accept full responsibility of citizenship, and are not doing so because of the privileges they enjoy by being classed as Indians.

Then may I suggest,
in order to take care of that individual, why can we not state in the act that when an Indian reaches a certain position he then must automatically become enfranchised?
That is exactly what this board is provided to determine.

This board may go into the Poundmaker reserve and take twenty or thirty or fifty Indians or take none at all. They can pick whom they like. You have a board consisting of two men who are officials of the department with the possibility, as my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie) says, of three appointed by the department, to force this on the Indian.

Not three members from
the department.

No, but you are going to have two, and another nominated by the department if the band does not choose one. I have had so much to do with the Indians and the problems facing the Indians in the disposition of the moneys that the Indian rightly thinks belong to him that I cannot conceive of the Indians as I know them even suggesting to the minister that this amendment be placed in the act.
I think probably some of us have a different viewpoint.

You have different
Indians, that is the trouble.

That is just what I was going to say. The Indians in my riding I think are probably ninety-nine per cent capable of conducting their business or exercising the franchise or anything else that the ordinary citizen of the community is capable of doing. I have some reason to believe, from conversation with others, that there are certain bands in the west and on the Pacific coast who have not that high intelligence and activity.

No, it is not lack of
intelligence, they are just as intelligent as your eastern Indians.

I say that that is what I have been informed. But some reference has been made by the ex-Minister of the Interior to the fact that they are wards of the government and have certain privileges. I think you have to go behind that a little. They exercise certain privileges because the government of the day is under certain obligations to them. We took the country from them, and the government pays them moneys in compensation, which moneys are doled out to the Indian at about $5 a month, and in times like these they think it is not sufficient, and it is not. A family of five gets $5 a month from the government, and we must remember that in times like these they are not given relief. They are wards of the Dominion government, and they are not given relief by the municipalities. As I endeavoured to point out the other day they are handicapped even when they go into the labour market. A year ago, when we were furnishing relief in the form of labour, the Indians could not get work because they are wards of the nation, and the other people in the community thought the Dominion government should look after them.
Will this amendment to the act make it any easier for the Indians?
I think so. I can only speak for my own district, but I think you will find that all the Indians in the constituency I represent will apply for enfranchisement right away.
Why have they not done so before now?

Perhaps it is a matter of education; perhaps they did not know they were entitled to do so. Really I cannot see any objection to the amendment. I think there should be an intelligence test, and I believe it should apply to others than Indians
To members of parliament.

Perhaps. The colour line should not be the line of distinction; that is my point. There should be an intelligence test, and if an Indian is sufficiently capable and intelligent why should he not be given the right to vote and why should he not be liable for any debts he may contract? Why not give him the full power of citizenship, as the Minister of Justice said; why not allow him to sell and buy things, even liquor if he wants it? I think this legislation is along the right line, and I believe it should pass.

Is this another case of the iron heel?

Indian Act

I think compulsory naturalization is a very dangerous thing, if that is what this amendment means. The minister admitted with some diffidence that this act will give him the power to enfranchise any Indian, and he explained the need for this power by pointing out cases of men who were in business. As the hon. member for North Bruce said, there would be no objection if the minister took that power only in regard to such people, but in answer to the hon. member the minister also said that he could apply it to entire bands if he so desired. When he was asked if he would apply it to Indians who did not want it he said their vigorous opposition would be taken into consideration. If the minister makes that statement in this house in view of the criticism which has been offered, it is quite evident that he realizes what is the fact, that he has absolute power to go out on a roving commission and enfranchise whom he likes. To quote scripture:
Whom he would he slew; and whom he would he kept alive.
Let us look at it from another point of view, a parallel case. There are a great many people in this country who are qualified for citizenship but who, for various reasons, do not avail themselves of that privilege. It would be a parallel case if we compelled these foreigners to become naturalized. If we can compel an Indian to become naturalized if that is the correct word, why should we not compel a Ukrainian or any other foreigner to accept the same responsibilities?

They are responsible
for their debts now.

I am speaking of exercising
the rights and privileges of citizens.
They have most of the rights and privileges also.

We talk largely of the advantages of being a Canadian citizen. Will we be proud to be associated with people who have been forced to become citizens? What will we think of the mental calibre and value of a citizen upon whom that privilege has been forced? This is a serious step to cake, but if we do it in the one case we may be asked to do it in the other as well. Why not simply take this power in cases which can be enumerated in another subsection, covering those men who are in business and who are exercising all the privileges of a white man, and leaving out the members of the bands who are neither willing nor able to become naturalized?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I was going to suggest
that we might frame a section permitting the Indian himself to apply for the franchise and another section to carry out the intent of this proposed amendment, giving the Superintendent General power in certain cases. That would allow the Indian to make application, and in cases where such application is not made the Superintendent General could make application on behalf of the Indian. If a double barrelled section of that kind would meet the situation I think one might be drafted.

May I point out that a
great deal of the objection from this side of the house has been to the compulsory enfranchisement of the Indians. An Indian has certain rights and privileges to which he is entitled. We took his country, and we owe him something. We came here and took away everything he had, and the least we can do is give him and his descendants some compensation in return. We have a treaty with him now, and I do not believe this parliament has the right, in justice and in common decency, to confer on the minister any power whatever to alter the terms of that treaty unless the Indian wants that step to be taken. The Indian has inherited certain privileges; he has become a ward of the government. He is not allowed to vote, presumably on the principle that there should be no taxation without representation. We say to him, however, "So long as you do not vote and do not become an ordinary citizen we will allow you to carry on as a ward of the government." Are we going to force him to vote? Are we going to take away from him the privileges which he has acquired traditionally and historically? I do not think we should do so, and I do not think the amendment proposed by the Minister of Justice should be introduced.

Before touching on the question involved in the amendment I should like to be clear on one point mentioned by the Minister of Justice, in regard to who actually is an Indian. I think the minister stated that an Indian was one who belonged to a band or an irregular band or who followed the Indian mode of life.

That is a non-treaty
Indian.

That is what I want
to have clear. My interpretation of the act- and I have been associated with Indians for the last fifty years and know a great deal about them-has been that an Indian who
Indian Act

was a non-treaty Indian and did not follow the Indian mode of life was a citizen of Canada. I should like to be clear on that point.
In the country that has been referred to by my hon. friend from North Timiskaming there are two distinct tribes of Indians who have intermingled. As far as one can leam, originally the Ojibway band, a section of the Algonquin tribe, occupied the height of land and the country south of the height of land and north of the great lakes. The Cree Indians occupied the watershed of Hudson bay and James bay. The Oree Indians in the Hudson bay area were one of the last bands to become treaty Indians; I think some of them did so quite recently. Before they became treaty Indians, however, and before they were recognized by the department in any sense, hundreds of them migrated from the shores of Hudson bay to the line of the Transcontinental railway and further south to the lake shore, and from the day they came to that district, some fifty years ago, they no longer followed the mode of life of the Indian. They stepped right in beside the white man and became citizens of the country, building homes for themselves and taking positions in railroad service, as mechanics and so on. In the town in which I live there is an Indian community living in homes as good as my own. They run locomotives; they have become telegraph operators, machinists and so on. They never have been recognized as Indians in the ordinary sense, as migratory or bush Indians, as we term them, have been recognized. That brings me to the situation referred to by the hon. member for North Timiskaming, where there are two classes of Indians. One of these classes exercise the franchise, and they have always done so, because they have never been recognized as wards of the government. I go a step further. We have a large Indian school three miles from the town in which I live, where the children of treaty Indians are entitled to free education in keeping with an arrangement made throughout Canada with the different denominations of the churches to which the Indians happen to belong. Now, the children of these Cree Indians are not entitled to the privileges of that Indian school, but their parents pay taxes to the public or the separate school as the case may be and they attend the school wherever it is located.
What is the situation with regard to these people? The term "following the Indian mode of life" has been applied to them although they do not follow that mode of life. People

commonly understand what that mode of life is; it means either that the Indians live on the reserve or that they are taking advantage of the privileges granted them to go hunting and fishing wherever they can. That is a point that should be definitely cleared up.
I come next to the question of the franchise. It is a fact that these Cree Indians have not for half a century followed the Indian mode of life but have lived after the manner of the white man, taking their position side by side with him and accepting all the responsibilities involved. One hon. gentleman referred to Indians who had gone overseas, and I believe I have stated in this house before that you could comb the country from the Mattawa river to the mountain line of Manitoba in 1917 and you could not find an adult Indian of military age and physically fit who had not volunteered to go overseas. But what is the situation when we come to enforce enfranchisement? The state is spending, to my personal knowledge, large sums of money on these Indian schools to train the boys and girls and fit them, not for the Indian mode of life but in order that they may, as their rights and privileges are taken away, and their opportunities disappear, step up alongside you or me or anyone else and take their position as Canadian citizens. But suppose they refuse to do this after all that has been done for them? I personally know of two girls who graduated from the Indian school in Chapleau. They were put through high school by the Indian department, through normal school by the Indian department, and they became qualified as school teachers, so that they are now teaching school in the southern part of Ontario in a settlement where all the children are white. Ultimately these young women will marry. There are men doing the same thing. In Chapleau, a young man, graduate of the Indian school and of the high school, takes a position in a bank or in a store or somewhere else. Should he not assume the responsibilities of citizenship when that has been done for him?
I know the Indians; at least I know two bands of Indians, having lived amongst them, and I know that they will be perfectly satisfied to allow their case to rest in the hands of the Indian department.
No, they won't.

I speak only of those I know, and I have had a lot to do with them. All this talk about the Indian department setting up a tribunal that will go among the bands of Indians and take some family and say to them, "You must be enfranchised," is all rot in my opinion. I have had a good deal

Indian Act
to do with the Indian department, for I was a member of the commission that approached that department many years ago and made the joint arrangement under which these schools from one end of Canada to the other are being carried on. The interest of the Indian department in the Indians, and the sympathetic manner in which they have dealt and are dealing with these people, are in my judgment a guarantee as to whether the rights of the Indians will be transgressed or not in any part of Canada. But after all these things have been done for them, if they insist on accepting one position that has been provided and refuse the other, then the Indian department should be clothed with responsibility and should say to them, "Now that we have brought you to this stage you must accept your responsibilities." I think the Minister of Justice should make that point clear with regard to these people. I know from personal knowledge that hundreds of them for the last forty or fifty years have been following the ordinary life of the white man and have not lived as Indians in any sense whatever. I am not a lawyer but I understand that the statute makes reference to treaty Indians, Indians living on a reserve, members of a band of Indians, or an irregular band, or men and women following the Indian's mode of life. But these people have not been following that mode of life in this generation, and many did not do so in the last.

I wish to say a word or two in answer to some remarks made by my hon. friend (Mr. Nicholson). There is a clear distinction between the rights in this country of what is known as the non-treaty Indian and those of the Indian as defined by the Indian Act. The treaty Indian obtained his rights as a result of treaties which were made, by which the government of this country agreed, as my hon. friend from Quebec South said, to give to the Indian certain protection in return for what was taken away from him. The non-treaty Indian stands in a different class; he belongs to what is known as an irregular band. That is a band that does not hold lands under location ticket, which is the way Indians belonging to bands hold their lands in this country. The non-treaty Indian belongs to an irregular band which has no land, and he is known as an Indian largely by the fact that he follows the Indian mode of life. He may be only a temporary resident in Canada.
Personally I would not object to the amendment which has been proposed being made applicable to non-treaty Indians because the country does not owe them the same obligations that were imposed upon the government by the treaties with the treaty Indians. There is a clear distinction. It is a breach of faith if the government of this country goes back on the rights which the Indians thought they obtained under their treaty, not merely with respect to the privileges that have been referred -to but with respect to what I regard as the greatest privilege of all which the Indian enjoys, namely, his privilege of being protected against the guile and cunning of the white man who makes certain deals with him that are not in his interest. That is why the Indian Act was drawn as it is. That is the reason that in this country we have not the right to issue execution against the lands of an Indian who is not a non-treaty Indian. Living on the border of a couple of reserves as I have done for many years, and knowing very intimately the difficulties in which the Indian becomes involved at the hands of the not-too-scrupulous white man, I say it is a grave breach of the fundamental principles that underlie the treaty between the representatives of the people of this country * and the Indians if you compulsorily take out of that class people who have for generations had that protection and say to them, "We will now compel you to become ordinary citizens and, whether you want it or not, to accept the obligations and responsibilities of white people to whom we owe no obligation such as we owe to you under our treaties." Every hon. member who lives near the borders of a reserve knows that some very attractive lands have been set aside for the Indians. These lands are particularly attractive because of the waters which run through them or the timber or the grasses which grow upon them. These lands are a credit to the people who selected them for the Indians. Certain portions of these lands may be wanted for timber or for pasture. The protection which the Indian has had in the past will be taken away by this amendment. Previously no man could obtain a lease of any land from an Indian without first having it approved by the Indian department. I do not think the minister realized what he was doing by removing this safeguard from the Indian. It is proposed to give him this land in fee simple and not to have it held in trust by the government.

Enfranchisement will be
given only after a proper investigation.
After it has been obtained in a way never hitherto intended.

Pardon me, a similar
amendment was passed in 1920.
Indian Act
No.

I beg the hon. member's
pardon, it was.

The minister does not get my point. This amendment contains for the first time the evil of which I complain. By it, an Indian can be compelled against his own will to be enfranchised and to be made liable to have his land and his chattels taken in execution. I ask the committee to listen to the provisions of the previous subsection, which reads:
Upon the application of an Indian of any band, or upon the application of a band on a vote of a majority of the male members of such band of the full age of twenty-one years at a meeting or council thereof summoned for that purpose, according to the rules of the band and held in the presence of the Superintendent General or of an officer duly authorized to attend such council, by the governor in council or by the Superintendent General, a board may be appointed by the Superintendent General to consist of two officers of the department and a member of the band to which the Indian or Indians under investigation belongs, to make inquiry and report as to the fitness of any Indian or Indians to be enfranchised.
It is proposed that the following be substituted for that subsection:
The Superintendent General may appoint a board to consist of two officers of the department and a member of the band to which the Indian or Indians under investigation belongs, to make inquiry and report as to the fitness of any Indian or Indians to be enfranchised.
The action would not be a voluntary one by the Indian, it would be compulsory and would be in violation of all treaties. The government would cease to be the protector of the Indian. He would be left at the mercy of crafty and designing people who wished to make contracts with him. It would be possible to obtain a judgment against an Indian which would have consequences which were not possible formerly. There has never been a time when the people need as much protection against sheriffs and executions. There has never been a time when the privileges enjoyed by our people, whether white people or Indians should be more carefully guarded than now. This action would be a terrible mistake and a breach of faith against this great body of people.
Many of the prizes given at the ploughing matches in western Ontario are won by Indian boys and by older Indians. These people are very capable in many ways but they are not so capable of taking care of themselves in the making of contracts. They should not be robbed of the protection that has been thrown round them for generations. In some cases they need to be protected from their own

improvidence. I would follow the suggestion made by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) to this extent, that this amendment should be limited to non-treaty Indians. We do not owe them the same obligation that we owe to the treaty Indians.
I do not think the Minister of Justice suggested that it should apply only to non-treaty Indians.

If the minister had been listening to me he would know that I did not suggest that the Minister of Justice made that statement. I am making a suggestion that it should be limited to non-treaty Indians because otherwise we would be guilty of a breach of the treaty. The Minister of Justice thought that a compromise might be arrived at and he suggested that they should be left the right to make application for enfranchisement and that there would also be the power in certain eases to compel them to accept enfranchisement. My suggestion is that the right of compelling enfranchisement should be limited to the non-treaty Indians. We should not go back on the obligations we undertook years ago to the ancestors of the present Indians.
The hon. member is in error when he makes the statement that this is the first time that such an amendment has been proposed.
If the minister will pardon me, I said that this subsection-

I did not interrupt my hon. friend and he should allow me to complete my remarks. He is in error when he says that this is the first time the proposal has been made to give this power to the Superintendent General and the department. This same amendment was passed in 1920 and it remained upon the statute books of this country for two years.
Why was it withdrawn?

I do not know what
motives actuated the minister at that time in taking that action. In order to make some progress and to meet the suggested amendment of the Minister of Justice, perhaps this section could stand for the time being.
How many Indians were enfranchised during the past two years?

I have not the figures for the last two years, I have them only for the last ten-year period. I do not think any

Indian Act
Indians were enfranchised during the last two years under this section; they were enfranchised under section 114, not under 110.
Is there a waiting list for the coming year?
There is not, under this section; there have been some applications made under section 114.

I have in my constituency the first colony composed entirely of graduates of the various Indian schools throughout the west. This colony has made great advancement in agricultural pursuits during the past thirty years. The main grievance I have from the members of this colony, especially on behalf of the sons of returned men, is that they have not been able to be enfranchised fast enough. An hon. member referred to that and a real question arises there. The sons of men who fought in the war and whose fathers are enfranchised by reason of their war service, are now in a number of cases of age and yet cannot vote. That is something I should like to see dealt with more satisfactorily than under this blanket clause whereby the minister and his officers can, in a wholesale way, take young Indians and old, and, just before an election, manufacture a lot of votes.
Very dangerous.
I am astonished at my hon. friends.
Oh, oh I

This would be the restoration of methods that prevailed many years ago, but in Saskatchewan we find the chief Conservative organizer, not on the relief commission, but administering the act as manager. If hon. members want to know his name, it is C. B. Daniels and a capable officer, but before he got the position he was chief Tory organizer in southern Saskatchewan. So we are just a little afraid that Saskatchewan methods may meander down here and be invoked by this government. I would ask the minister not to put himself into that position, because I do not believe he wants to be put in it. That is exactly what may happen, however.
Another point is that these Indians who have been dispossessed of their property, by force if you like, but more humanely in Canada than in any other country, are going to be weaned at a time the most difficult I can remember to be put on their own. I have been telling these young men who are anxious
to be enfranchised, that they are better off to-day than the white man. They have their schools near by, hospitals, medical services and an advisory foreman over them. They have every possible aid of which one can conceive. Now at this time when nobody can make a living on the farm, or at least nobody can pay his debts or replace his machinery, the government, under the guise of enfranchising these Indians, is going to shove them on their own wholesale. There must be some compelling force behind this enfranchisement conception under those inhuman conditions to which I have referred. I cannot conceive of any of them wanting the franchise on such terms as having to pay taxes and so on like the white man and hustling around under conditions that are very difficult, even though they do not start with any debts. I would ask my hon. friend not to have such terms embodied in this section. Let us give the young men as well as the old the right of initiative in making their own reforms. No individual can become a member of a band without the consent of its council. If an Indian from some other reserve wants to become a member of a band, he has to obtain the consent of the majority in it. When my hon. friend is looking into this matter, let him consider also the situation of the wives of these returned men. Nobody knows whether they have votes or not. In some places they vote; in others they do not. What about the wives of any of the Indians who are going to be enfranchised? Why should the franchise be confined to the males only? The Indian women are frequently better workers than the males.
They support the men,

Of course. As the saying goes:	The woman is the better man
of the two. They certainly deserve as much recognition as do the males in regard to enfranchisement, and they are quite as capable of exercising it intelligently. I think the minister should leave the section as it is, that is, preserve the right of voluntary enfranchisement.

In the constituency which
I represent there are no Indians, either treaty or otherwise, and I rise to say a few words only on behalf of what I regard as a very definite principle. The term "treaty Indians" has been used. That implies, to me at least, although I have no extensive knowledge of this particular subject, that some sort of contract has been made with those Indians. If such a contract has been made, surely it is
Indian Act

not right for one party to it to break it without the consent of the other, or, in other words, to treat it as a scrap of paper of which we heard so much in days gone by.
Moreover, I am constitutionally opposed to anything in the nature of compulsion. I do not like the thought that men shall become naturalized against their will. Further, if they have not a sufficient appreciation of the rights of the franchise, of citizenship, to make the application themselves, I doubt very much whether it is worth while to make them citizens. I would add this as a qualification: If you are going to do that, I see no reason, as the hon. member for Comox-Albemi has said, why you should make a distinction, naturalizing Indians because they are worthy of being citizens, intelligent, industrious, and should assume all the responsibilities as well as possess all the advantages of citizenship, and not apply the same rule in the case of foreigners who have been in this country for five years or more, who have all the qualifications of citizenship and who yet do not avail themselves of their right to become naturalized. I might even go so far as this, that as regards men from other countries, I do not care where they come from, from the white countries if you like, from the countries of Europe, who have made Canada their permanent home and who for some reason do not become naturalized, it ought to be brought to their attention that it is their duty to assume all the responsibilities of citizenship. I should not make naturalization difficult in cases of that kind. Perhaps I am going a little too far afield in saying that. Instead of making it difficult for these men to become naturalized if they are willing to become citizens, I would make it easy.
I rose more particularly to dwell upon what my deskmate said a moment or two ago. I do not ordinarily attribute sinister motives to anyone. I remember very well some seven or eight years ago when the Hon. Mr. Copp, who is now in the Senate, was Secretary of State and as such introduced an amendment to the Naturalization Act under which the Secretary of State was empowered to naturalize those who applied instead of the procedure before the judges as is the case at present. I recall what severe resistance was offered by our Conservative friends who were then in opposition. They gave as their reason that it would be very easy, just prior to an election, for a secretary of state, at the behest of a government that naturally wanted to be reelected, to naturalize these foreigners in shoals and hordes, in hundreds and thousands, knowing all the time they would vote in a

way that would be advantageous to the government. I do not say that would be done in this case, but as my hon. friend to my right says, it becomes possible for a government so to act. The amendment was withdrawn. The only reason that has been given by the minister for the introduction of this amendment is that there are a few Indians who have refused to pay their just obligations and who have taken refuge behind their privileges. I would say to him: While that argument may be sound, I do not think it is of sufficient importance; I do not think the instances would be so numerous-I believe they would be very few-as to justify him in breaking a sacred treaty with those Indians.

A moment ago I asked that this clause might stand in order that the suggestion made by the Minister of Justice might be considered and we might make some progress. I have no desire to shut off discussion; further discussion may be had at the next sitting. Perhaps we would make greater progress with another clause.

My answer to that is that there are in the criminal code at present sections sufficient for the purpose. There are all the sections concerning sedition and unlawful rioting. The danger in this legislation lies in the fact that it may be used against organized labour. Legitimately organized unions and organized labour have in years gone by protested against this legislation.
