maintopic: SUPPLY-INSPECTION OF CANNED SALMON STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a few words about a subject of considerable importance to the fishing industry of British Columbia. My remarks arise from the passing on the third day of this month of order in council No. 206. I should like to discuss the matter from two angles, first the ostensible reason put forward for its passage and then I should like to state what I believe to be the real and ulterior motive behind iC
Before doing that however I should like to deal with the method of introducing the order in council. Although it was passed on February 3, it was not gazetted until fifteen days later, namely on February 18. However the public was, so to speak, privately advised of it, and hon. members from British Columbia who were here at the seat of government had to get their information that the order in council had become law from the newspapers published in the west, which were sent to us from British Columbia. While the order in council is vital to the fishing interests, it was actually passed under the authority of the Meat and Canned Foods Act. A section of that act is devoted to fishing matters, and is under the control of the Minister of Fisheries. I suggest therefore that the responsibility for the passing of this order in council is his.
I should like to give three reasons why it should not have been introduced in that way. In the first place the matter to which I have reference should never have been introduced as an order in council. It was of sufficient importance to be introduced as a bill. We are all familiar with the law-I believe it is a law-that regulations under an act must be confined entirely to amplifying or carrying out the purposes of that act, and that it is ultra vires by way of order in council to introduce that which is practically a new law. We are told that any change of that kind must be brought about by means of a new act. Comment is often made by hon. members on both sides of the house that the party sitting opposite is merely rubber stamping the opinions of the government or of t.he opposition as the case may be. That may be so, but at least on such occasions we are rubber stamping opinions and policies decided either in a meeting of the cabinet, at a party caucus or at a convention. But there is another aspect in connection with which we are all equally guilty, and which constitutes a worse form of rubber stamping. The government brings a bill before the house under which it takes power to pass regulations; thereafter all our responsibility and control seems to disappear. We simply come
here and find that the government has rubber stamped the views and opinions of one or two officials, that action has been taken in secrecy and without any publicity. If that is not rubber stamping carried to excess, I do not know what it is.
In 1932, about a year ago, there was a complete revision of the Fisheries Act. That matter was referred to the marine and fisheries committee, and under the chairmanship of the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Ernst) good work was done. A considerable part of the work in that committee was merely that of revision. But in addition some new sections were introduced, passed and reported to the house. But not one of those new sections, or even the whole of them put together, had the importance of this order in council which has now been slipped through without publicity of any kind. All that work was done, and now we find an order in council is passed which might possibly vitiate some of the most important parts of the act itself.
I object, again, to the fact that the order in council was passed when the house was sitting. About the year 1923 a resolution was passed in the marine and fisheries committee of which the hon. member for Antig-onish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff) was chairman. That resolution was to the effect-and he will correct me if I am wrong-that the committee requested or recommended-the language was not more imperative than that-that if the department proposed to put through any order in council relating to fishery matters while the house was sitting, the committee should first be advised. The idea was that parliament was paramount, and that while parliament was sitting and the committee was sitting it would be wise and well that any material changes proposed to be enacted by order in council should receive the investigation of the committee. I submit that the change to which I shall refer 'is very material, and should have been referred to that committee. There could have been no rush, because the action proposed to be taken could not possibly be taken for three months, and more likely about four and a half months. There was no excuse for the secret rush- because I believe that is the way to describe it.
My third objection is that it is a breach of good faith with the whole fishing industry of British Columbia. In the last eight or nine years a most admirable practice has grown up in the department, whereby the minister or his deputy has visited British Columbia once a year, mostly in the early
Inspection oj Canned Salmon

days of December. The present Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) came one year, and we were pleased to see him. On such occasions the deputy minister holds meetings at three or four of the principal points in British Columbia. An agenda is prepared beforehand, and any person, whether he be rich or poor, canner-man or fisherman, is entitled to place his views before the meeting. All people are welcome, canner-men, fishermen and dealers. The result is that the officials receive an idea of the feelings in the industry. The meetings have been found so satisfactory that a practice has grown up, established by long usage, that unless a matter has been discussed at one of the meetings it will not, except in very urgent oases, be made the subject of legislation during the coming year. That met the objection that was so common for many years that the government had a habit, influenced perhaps by political or other considerations, of passing orders in council and legislation of that kind at the very last minute. The canneries were embarrassed by these regulations coming in the last minute before the season began; the fishermen did not know what regulations they had to comply with; so it became a well established rule that unless it was something of extreme urgency, nothing that had not been discussed at these meetings would become the subject of orders in council for the ensuing season. That has been carried out for eight or nine years with very good results. It was departed from on one occasion last year, a matter of political influence, very much to be regretted, and here we have another departure and a very much worse one. Last year when the deputy was out in December he had four meetings at least, five possibly, and discussed matters fully. The agenda I am of course quite familiar with. There was nothing in the agenda about this subject, it was never brought up at any of the meetings, the deputy minister never heard of it as far as we know, and no hint was given of anything of the kind. Early in January I heard a whisper -these things do leak out-that an attempt was to be made to put over this legislation -and "put over" is precisely the language to use. I wrote to the department on the 13th of January and got an answer dated the 20th of January which indicates that my letter was the first intimation that had reached the department about this matter. Then it goes on to say that the requirement that none other than salmon in perfect condition should be placed in cans was being well taken care of through the inspection of 
canned fish. Well, that reassured me; I was satisfied then that there was nothing in the whispers that I had heard.
So that on January 20 the department had no intention of legislating along the lines of the order in council which it passed two weeks later. I do not suppose they get up before breakfast to pass an order in council; it must have been a matter of consideration, possibly of correspondence. At any rate within two weeks after the date on which the department assured me there was nothing in the wind the order in council was actually signed by His Excellency-without publicity, and it was not put into the Gazette until fifteen days later. Why was no notice given the industry? Why were the independent can-ners, who were going to be deeply affected, not advised? Why were the fishermen, whose livelihood was imperilled to a large extent, not advised? I might even say, why was I not advised, considering that I had been assured fourteen days before that there was nothing in it at all? I think it would have been only fair to advise me of this sudden change of principle and policy and as to what their intentions were. I keep asking myself again and again, why was this thing perpetrated? Why? Why? Well, sir, I can answer my own question. For the same reason that a burglar operates in the dark; it had to be put over in the dark because it could not be done in the daylight. The least breath of publicity, the merest ray of light thrown upon it, would have killed it. Now I want to be perfectly fair. Sometimes I am accused of not being fair, but I am. I see the acting Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Duranleau) quite agrees with my contention, though I do not know which one it is he agrees with. I am sure it is the first one. At any rate I want to be fair to-day, and I will say that the defence given by the department-I do not know if I am paying them a compliment when I say defence-is this, that the order in council dealt with the inspection of canned salmon, and as this inspection of canned salmon is a matter wholly concerning the oanners it was not necessary to take it up at these meetings on the coast attended by fishermen and others, and therefore all I have said about not passing legislation that was not considered at these meetings was beside the mark. Yes, it is true that ostensibly it deals only with canned salmon inspection regulations, and if that was true in its entirety, then consulting the oanners alone would have sufficed. But it is a terrible and obvious quibble. The nature of this regulation is such that it becomes of vital

Inspection oj Canned Salmon
and desperate importance to the fishermen, and that places it in the category of the things that should have been discussed at the fishermen's meetings. So that dissipates that defence.
To sum up: First, this legislation should have been introduced by an act; second, it should have been referred to the marine and fisheries committee then sitting; and third, it was a breach of the established policy that had been carried out for years and years with the fishing industry in British Columbia.
Now having dealt with the circumstances surrounding the illegitimate birth of this- might I call it-piscatorial foundling, let us devote ourselves to some consideration of the reasons alleged in support of its original conception. Ostensibly it was introduced to strengthen the government regulations dealing with the inspection of canned salmon. Years ago the government found it necessary, and properly so, to install a system of government inspection and guarantee of canned salmon. The question immediately arose as to how to accomplish that inspection. Two ways were suggested. A number of people recommended, and I think I supported them, that it could best be done by having one inspector at every cannery. He would stand there, he would see the fish as it came in; it would matter not to him where it came from or how long it had been caught, or anything else; all he would be guided by would be his judgment of the actual state of the fish. If the fish were bad he would say: That fish must not be canned. If he gave his approval to it being canned-he was there in the plant and would have followed every detail of the procedure; it is a well known process-at the end of the process he would be able in all sincerity to give a certificate that it was of the first class. That would have been the best idea, but the government found it to be too costly. I agree with them; possibly it was. So they decided upon the other method -there were practically only two between which to choose-that is making the test on the canned product. I emphasize that because my whole objection turns upon it. The government decided that the inspection would be made on the canned product. So many tins would be opened and the inspector would pass judgment on it, just as you do in the case of fruit or other articles. Now last April the government in pursuance of this policy introduced by order in council under the Meat and Canned Foods Act a considerable number of regulations dealing with the inspection of canned salmon. It will be recalled that I objected very strenuously to some of them,
not that I objected to the system, but I said they were unworkable, ill calculated to achieve the object they professed to serve. Of course no attention was paid to my protest; they were declared to be perfect. The impression was given that they were inspired. Well, Mr. Speaker, they may have been inspired, but I do not think they were divinely inspired. The inspiration came from a less exalted source. To use the vernacular, I have since got quite a kick out of the subsequent results of those supposedly inspired regulations that could not be improved upon and were the very last word. The thing became, as I had predicted, a joke-simply and plainly a joke. A gentleman came out from London, England, one of the biggest buyers of canned salmon in the world-and that is a big word. He had a very big older with him. He expressed in plain English, very emphatic language that I could hardly repeat here, his opinion of the intelligence and mental capacity of anyone who would consider those regulations suitable or useful. He said that for his part he was not going to buy a case of salmon unless it passed the inspector arranged by himself. Since then I have received information from a gentleman of some standing in Australia who complained 'that the regulations had lent themselves to direct abuse. That was in the early days, before the regulations were amended. He said they encouraged people to take salmon of an inferior grade to Australia, where it was sold as the very best, and a little later I will quote from his letter.
Perhaps the best proof of the futility of these regulations can be shown by the way the department treated its love child. The regulations were put in operation ten months ago, and since then they have been amended five times. The original regulations covered two and a half columns of the Gazette, but the five amendments or additions made since then extend to some five and a third columns. In other words it has been found necessary to patch or add to this good and godly garment until the patches cover the garment not once but two and a half times. That will give us some idea of the adequacy of the original regulations. These amendments were made to a very considerable extent along the lines I advocated. Of course they did not follow my recommendations too closely; that would not have done at all. There is such a thing as saving the face of the department, and it would not have done to give me an opportunity to say "I told you so" too plainly. At any rate the amendments were substantially along the lines I suggested. Finally the officials thought the regulations
Inspection of Canned Salmon

were now all right, at least they thought so until three weeks ago, when they threw this order in council into the works and upset everything again. Let me quote the letter of the department dealing with these regulations:
... it may be said, without the possibility of successful contradiction, . . .
That is a brave statement.
. . . that the fact that the original regulations and the amendments thereto have been accepted with remarkably near unanimity by the canners, is in itself an evidence of the efficiency of the regulations.
Is it really? It is to laugh. It might also be held to be evidence of the fact that the reglations were so ineffective that the people concerned did not bother to complain of them. It might be taken to mean that they were glad to get the appearance of government endorsation of their product even though the regulations were so feeble and ineffective that they did not impose any restriction on them. Suppose I were asked to formulate a set of regulations to deal with a case of smuggling, and later I had to make a report. I might say, "Well, I have a set of regulations that have worked like a charm. The smugglers are perfectly satisfied with them." Would that be considered an evidence of efficiency? I rather doubt it, yet that is all it amounts to. For evidence of that kind I would rather look to statements by buyers and wholesalers in other countries. I would look to see if these Englishmen were content to accept the government inspection and no longer insist on their own inspection.
At any rate, that is the official attitude. We have further endorsation from British Columbia. The chief supervisor of fisheries is quoted as follows:
It has proved a notable success and has been welcomed by overseas buyers, especially in Great Britain and Australia.
Then I see a long article in the Pacific Fisherman, a well known fisheries paper, in which the chief supervisor is quoted as follows:
The results, he said, have been in general highly satisfactory, and the buying trade has been well pleased;-
Then follow endorsations by two or three of the leading cannery operators in British Columbia. That must have been a red letter day for the chief supervisor of fisheries. In addition to having his views recorded on one page, I find on an adjoining page a really pretty photograph of him attired in the most up-to-date golfing togs and associating with some of the leading cannery operators on the coast, an attitude which I 
think is highly symbolic. It was rather curious to hear the chief supervisor talk about the results being so satisfactory in Australia, because I have in my hand a letter written last November by a man who says he is the representative of a large merchandising business in Australia, the name of which he mentions. He says:
For some time past, several merchants have been relabelling salmon, mostly pinks, and naming them reds and distributing them as reds. The practice, apart from its dishonesty and misrepresentation, was causing bona fide traders concern, especially those who would not practise the deception.
Then in a letter he sent to the government of Australia he says:
I understand the federal government of Canada was trying to make it an offence under the pure foods department or health act, but the results are very disappointing.
But the chief supervisor says he has had word that the results are very satisfactory.

speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman mind letting me see that letter?

maintopic: SUPPLY-INSPECTION OF CANNED SALMON STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Certainly. Part of it is a personal letter to myself, but I know my hon. friend will treat it as such.
Among the regulations passed last April was one establishing a board of inspectors. I objected to that system very strongly, because it appeared that these inspectors who were liable to condemn the packs of the canners to the extent of thousands of dollars were to be nominated, appointed and paid by the canners themselves. Is it any wonder that I objected to a system of that kind? I have in my hand a clipping from the journal published by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, in which comment is made on the system of inspecting meat in Australia. I find these words:
All these inspectors are salaried officers of the commonwealth government entirely independent of the proprietors of the meat works.
Is that not the proper way? How would it look if this same journal, published by the government, in explaining the system of salmon inspection had to say that these inspectors were nominated, appointed and paid by the canners themselves? What weight has an inspection conceived and carried on in this way? I will say, however, as I said in April last, that by chance or otherwise the first men appointed to the board were good, capable, competent and reliable men, whose integrity and honesty is unquestioned. I am not saying a word against them. I said then, and I repeat, that I would be quite satisfied with their judgment as such, but I do condemn the system. We left it to the judgment of

Inspection of Canned Salmon
these good men; we said to them, "You will look at this salmon. If in your judgment it is good you will pass it." Here are the exact words of the order in council defining the duties of these men; it is subsection 27 (a):
Canned salmon that are found by the board of inspection to be fresh, firm, well-packed and in good, merchantable condition, shall be approved and a certificate in the form attached marked A shall be issued therefor.
If the inspector found that the fish was in that condition in the tin, fresh, firm, well-packed and in good, merchantable condition, he would issue the certificate, but if he did not issue the certificate, if it were anything inferior to that standard, it had to be marked second quality, and that absolutely damned the sale of it, because you cannot sell canned fish marked second quality.
That was the section under which these men acted; it was within their sound judgment as to whether the fish complied with that requirement. Now I come to the order in council which was passed on February 3 last. It simply added a proviso to the words I have just read, as follows:
Provided that no certificate shall be issued for canned salmon that had not been landed fresh at a cannery for canning within twenty-four hours after being caught, excepting fish that has been gutted and iced immediately after being caught.
They have their tenses mixed; it is not even grammatical. However we will let that go. You will observe that it stipulates that the fish must be landed at the cannery fresh for canning within twenty-four hours of being caught. It does not say that it must be canned within twenty-four hours, so that vitiates the usefulness of the whole provision right there, to say nothing of other reasons that might be advanced. It may be landed at the cannery within twenty-four hours, but the fish may lie there for another twelve hours to suit the convenience of the cannery man, because there is nothing to prevent that being done.
In the preamble of the order in council it is stated:
Whereas the acting Minister of Fisheries, on the advice of the deputy Minister of Fisheries and the responsible officers of the department, and with the approval-
With the approval of whom?
-of the salmon canners, recommends that, etc. . . .
It is with the approval of the salmon canners, the very people whose goods are to be inspected and perhaps severely dealt with. That order in council creates an absolute departure from the principles that the government had already laid down. Formerly the
test was simply the appearance and condition of the fish. The question that had to be decided was, did it comply with that stipulation that it should be fresh, firm, well-packed and in good merchantable condition. It was left to the judgment of competent, experienced, reliable men. They did not have to consider the history of the salmon or its pedigree or ancestry, or where it came from or anything else. It might have come from California or Mexico or the Arctic pole; all they had to do was to use their judgment and determine whether it was of the required quality. If it did they would approve; if not, they would not. What is the situation now? They may be perfectly prepared to approve it; the fish may come up to every word of that requirement; but if in addition to that it is not proved that the fish has been delivered at the cannery within twenty-four hours of its being caught then it must be condemned.
Now how are these men to know whether the fish has been delivered within that time or not? It might have been delivered within ten hours of being caught and still it might be the duty of the inspector on inspection to condemn it; that would be quite understandable. But what is the test? Is it delivery within twenty-four hours of the fish being caught, or is the test to be the question whether or not the fish comes up to the stipulated requirement that it shall be fresh, firm, well-packed and in good merchantable condition? There is no question at all that in the final analysis this last is the principle on which the inspectors must act. If it is bad, it is the inspector's duty to condemn it even though the fish may have been put into the tin alive. But if on the other hand the inspector finds that it is perfectly good, quite fresh and of the highest quality, he cannot give a certificate unless it can be proved that the fish was landed at a cannery within twenty-four hours of being caught. Now I should like to know how any inspector can get that information? Why the need for this sudden and violent change of policy, changing the whole system right round, from the inspection of the canned product to a question as to the time within which the fish has been delivered at the cannery?
The system was lovely; the department at Ottawa said so. The chief supervisor in British Columbia says so, and he is the last word as an authority on fish, certainly in his own opinion. This was not asked for by the officials; at any rate it was not asked for by them as late as January 20, because I have the letter right here. It was not asked for by the board of inspectors. Now would you
Inspection of Canned Salmon

not have expected to find the inspectors taking part in this and approving of the order in council? Yet there is no record in the order in council, in the correspondence or anywhere else to show that they were either interested in, or invited to express any opinion on the subject. They did not ask for it, and it would have been remarkable had they done so, because it would have been admitting openly an obvious reflection on their ability and intelligence. Who then did ask for this change in the system? It was not the department; it was not the inspectors; it was not the fishermen. I will tell you who did ask for it. According to the letter from the department, strong representations were made to the department on behalf of those who put up over ninety per cent of the canned product-not ninety per cent of the canners, but those who put up ninety per cent of the canned product, which might have represented two or three companies-
-that- the existing inspection requirements that canned salmon must be fresh, firm, well packed and in good merchantable condition to be entitled to a certificate were not sufficient.
And it had to be buttressed up in the way I have indicated. Why did they ask this? Were they dissatisfied with the judgment of their own inspectors whom they themselves had recommended so strongly only ten months before? Was there any reason for dissatisfaction with them? Had any word come back from the markets in Britain and elsewhere that the fish was not in proper condition and that the regulation as it stood was inadequate? No sign cur evidence of that at all. I will give the real reasons in a moment.
Let us consider how this requirement will work, or rather not work. How will it be carried out? Is there to be an inspector on every little boat, a man who will stand there and put a tag on every salmon as it comes on board, or how will he know? Are you going to make the fisherman, when he comes to the cannery, take an oath as to how long this particular fish or that other fish has been out of the water? I have a vision of a man coming in with twenty or thirty fish and taking an oath that these eighteen fish over here had been caught sixteen hours, those six with the curly tails had been caught a couple of hours later, and as to this other lot over here, well perhaps they had been caught twenty-five hours but he was on daylight saving time while the officials were on standard time, so perhaps that would make it all right. Or are you going to require an oath of the cannery man? Of what use would that be? He could not know. He could only repeat what the fisherman had told him. I am not impugning
[Mr. Neill.l
the honour or integrity of the cannery man, but we all know that in any rank of life if you make it compulsory for people to swear to stereotyped statements it will simply mean that some bookkeeper will say, "Here Bill, sign this thing," and Bill will sign it, although he does not know what it refers to. I have known cases-and I am not referring now to the fish business-where one man has been required to sign something and in his absence someone else has signed his name.
I contend therefore that this provision will be entirely superficial. It will be entirely useless, and stereotyped statements forced in that way are of little value anyhow. I want you to note this also. The inspector may be perfectly willing to O.K. the fish but he has to have evidence that they were landed on the wharf twenty-four hours after they were caught. How is he to get it? He must get it or else the whole thing must be a joke and never intended to be enforced. I rather suspect that, in this aspect of it, and I intend to suggest a real reason. How is this thing going to be done? The order in council which I read contains no provision by which it can be carried out. The order in council was passed on February 3, four months before it was needed, and yet no method was suggested for carrying out its provisions. How is he to find out whether the fish was caught within the time? It is unworkable and it is superfluous. It would be superfluous if it were not unworkable and it would be unworkable if it were not superfluous-it is both.
The argument is used that after all twenty-four hours is a long time and a considerable distance can be covered in that period. Time is a comparative thing. If a man is to be hanged, twenty-four hours is a different measure of time than if he is going to be married. It is said that you can go two hundred miles in twenty-four hours, but that means eight and a quarter miles per hour which would require a faster boat than is generally used. Fish cannot be caught like you would go into a store to buy a pound of butter. Fishing is not one incidental, isolated action, it may take twelve or fifteen hours to get a load. If the first part of the load happens to be just within the twenty-four hours, the latter must be within the eight or ten hours. Such a provision would impose a hardship upon the fishermen. Then, as every fisherman knows, it depends entirely upon how the catch is handled. An inspector might properly reject fish which had been only ten hours out of the water. So many factors enter into this matter; there is the variety of fish and the conditions under which they are caught, the weather, icing and so on.

Inspection oj Canned Salmon
The fish must be landed upon the cannery wharf within twenty-four hours, but only landed. What use is that? The idea in mind is supposed to be quality, but how can the quality be improved by insisting that the fish be landed upon the wharf within twenty-four hours after being caught and then permitting them to remain upon the wharf twenty-four hours more. There is no provision to take care of that possibility. The only provision is that the fish must be landed upon the wharf within twenty-four hours.
It is a well known fact to those who know, and the men behind this movement, do know, that some fish carry much better than others. I am told that sockeye carry much better in the round, that is, unopened and ungutted, than other fish do even when gutted and iced. There is something about sockeye which makes them carry better without opening. They do not feed immediately before being caught and are not full of what is called red feed which ferments and decays. Let me quote from a practical cannoryman, as follows:
It is a fact that sockeyes for instance oarvy better in the round than any other species of salmon, having no feed in them, and we are prepared to guarantee that we will land sockeyes properly iced in the round seventy-two hours after being caught in better condition than similar fish landed twenty-four hours after being caught which have not been properly eared for and iced.
To my own knowledge I know that that is true. As I said before, the conditions imposed by the order in council are superfluous, useless and unworkable. I doubt very much if there will be any genuine attempt made to enforce them. It will be a dead letter, there are no teeth in it as regards its ostensible purpose.
I shall now deal with the other purposes of the regulation and to do this I shall have to go back a little into the history of the canning industry of British Columbia. Many years ago there were no canneries, the waters were open to everyone and to everything. Certain men b^gan to can and it was thought desirable to encourage them. The thing was an uncertain venture and the government quite properly gave them the exclusive rights to large bodies of water. I am not kicking against that action because I probably would have done the same thing as there did not seem to be any reason at that time for not doing it. Unfortunately, where you create a monopoly, in time you lead to favouritism and graft. The worst feature of the whole proceeding was that it gave not only exclusive rights to canning but also to fishing. It is hard to believe that only fourteen years ago it was a criminal offence for a Canadian
to go out into territorial waters-I think it applied also to extraterritorial waters-and catch fish. He could not get a licence or if he did it would be of no use to him. The cannerymen received and farmed out the fishing licences to the fishermen who were in a state bordering upon economic serfdom. They were absolutely at the dictation and the influence of the men from whom, and from whom only they could get the licence which enabled them to fish. The canning trade proved to be profitable and many petitions were made to obtain the rights which at that time could be obtained only by political influence.
In 1917 or 1918, I just forget which, the Hon. Mr. Rallantyne, Minister of Fisheries in the Union government, went out to the west coast. I am glad to note that in the parliamentary guide book he puts his politics down as Independent, and this perhaps accounts for the courage and foresight with which he acted. To paraphrase Genesis, he saw that the thing was not good and he put his foot down and said: I will do away with all this. He established an open door policy, so that everyone who bought a licence and complied with the conditions could go and fish and carry on as a canneryman or fisherman. The fishermen could then call their souls their own, they ceased to be criminals when they went fishing. They had a standing in the community, they saved money and bought their own boats. They became a sturdy and desirable class of citizens, they married and settled with their families to form little fishing communities. They represent a bulwark of empire upon our western front. Some day some nation-I am not indicating which-may want to form another Manchukuo on Vancouver island. It may be said that that is impossible, but we thought the other Manchukuo was impossible. From an imperial and national point of view it is very desirable to have these little settlements along the narrow waters and fjords. These sturdy, hardy fishermen are thoroughly familiar with the waters of the western coast.
Another result, perhaps not as desirable, which followed this open-door policy was the increase in the number of canneries. People rushed into the business and before long there were jealousies and rivalries between the different canneries. It led also to very intensive fishing. To equip properly a seine boat costs from $20,000 to $25,000. Previously, two canneries located in comparative proximity were in the habit of each putting in, say a couple of seines. However, in order to make more money and to get ahead of the other
Inspection oj Canned Salmon

fellow-the undying horror of a canneryman is to let a neighbour get half a fin ahead of him-they went out and put four seines each into the water. Then the other fellow would try to go one better and I have heard of cases where fifteen seines have been placed in waters which would ordinarily take only four. The department, realizing the danger to the industry brought about by this action, formulated a rule that if more than a reasonable number of seines were being used, the department to be the judge, the number of days for fishing per week would be cut down. Of course by this method you get more fish. But it was far more expensive fish; it cost the eaoners more money to get a given quantity by these intensive methods. You can imagine that catching one-third more fish with five times the equipment would not be profitable. The rivalries and jealousies led also to fish of poorer or more doubtful quality being put up. The one idea in those years seemed to be to get a bigger and bigger pack regardless of the cost and heedless of the quality of the fish put up. This meant a huge outlay for the boats and a bankrupting outlay for the canners. By and by the inevitable result followed of heavy losses. Backers and bankers began to ask:	Why all this sudden
loss? Why this large expenditure? Like the Israelites of old, who when they were cornered in the wilderness as a result of their sins, instead of acknowledging them, cried: Would to God we had stayed with the fleshpots in Egypt, the cannerymen, because it is not human nature to admit one is wrong, instead of admitting the facts as they were, said: It is all due to Ballantyne's malicious policy; if we could only get back to the good old days when there was the closed door and exclusive rights all round, when I owned this fifty miles of seaboard and you owned the other, everything would be all right.
In fulfilment of those views, which the backers and bankers had to accept in lieu of a better and more definite statement, they tried to get back the good old days. They made a perfectly legitimate effort by endeavouring to have the Dominion government alter its policy. Succeeding governments were approached, and quite properly, but all efforts were unsuccessful. Then they attempted to work it through the provincial government, it having acquired rights over canneries and the fish after they were caught. The Hon. Mr. Howe, who was minister in charge, in a very roundabout way sought to give them the advantage for which they asked, but the method he proposed was so nonsensical that after it had been threshed out in committee of the local house, the cannery men's own 
lawyers advised him to withdraw it because if he attempted to put it through, it would only make his ignorance of the subject all the more apparent.
Following this, less creditable methods were adopted. They said: If we cannot get it by means of change of policy, of legislation, perhaps we can get it by means of regulations which say one thing and mean another. What they wanted to do of course was to get back as near as they could to the good old days, eliminate the small independent canners that had sprung up among the old established ones and also eliminate the independent fishermen who weTe growing in strength and importance, and make them serfs and tools of the cannerymen and dependent on them. This meant huge expenditures in boats and so forth. The really proper policy for the canners to adopt is to encourage the independent fishermen and let them fish and let the cannery men can. In all phases of industry it has been a good system not to try to do too many things at once. So the independent fishermen should be encouraged instead of being discriminated against. In this way the cannerymen would be saved great outlays and they could devote themselves to their business which is sufficiently large and profitable under normal conditions for them to pay their whole attention to it. It is needless to say that all these recommendations and proposals were made in the name of conservation and quality. Someone has said:	O patriotism, what crimes are committed in thy name! I have had a long and wide acquaintance with fishermen and cannerymen and every other class of the industry, and not one of them, when asking for something to which he was not entitled, has not laid his argument on the altar of conservation and quality. That is a proverbial and well known fact.
Mr. Speaker, as I have finished this phase of my argument, I would ask you to call it six o'clock.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock. PRIVATE BILL

maintopic: SUPPLY-INSPECTION OF CANNED SALMON STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the hour for private bills expired on Friday evening I was just about to congratulate the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) on his success, at least to his own satisfaction, in answering charges made by hon. members opposite to the effect that there was some connection between the group to which he belongs, or groups in this corner of the house, and the communistic organizations of Canada. While I wish to congratulate him upon his success in satisfying his own mind, I am very much afraid that his was a labour of love which will remain unrequited for a long time, because hon. gentlemen opposite who insist upon making the charge would be very much disappointed if they had to accept the truth, which is that there never has been and never can be any connection between these groups and communistic organizations.
It appears to me that perhaps one reason why a certain section of the house opposes the repeal of section 98 is in order that it might be used for political purposes. By inspiring fear they hope to accomplish that which they cannot accomplish by applying reason. Such terms as bolshevism, communism and revolution used by people who have 53719-147
political objects in view present alarming pictures to the general public. Each one of those words in the minds of some people stands for something quite objectionable. Their connotations are such as to inspire fear and repulsion. So, in a movement in this country if one manages to connect with it the terms bolshevism, communism and revolution, he immediately raises an unreasoned objection on the part of the general public. It is very much like witchcraft. I suppose there never was actually such a thing as witchcraft, yet many poor old women paid with their lives for that superstitution. I do not suppose there is any real revolutionary movement in Canada; certainly those in this corner who are charged with being revolutionary are not. And yet this suggestion is being used, just as witchcraft was used, to scare people.
As I have said, perhaps that is one reason why some hon. gentlemen wish to retain section 98. They keep it alive for political purposes. I am not so sure that government agents are not employed in certain parts of Canada to stir up strife, in order that section 98 might be used. Certainly we have had examples of this in Leopold and Zanetti. These gentlemen were government-paid agents who took an inside leadership in certain communistic movements of Canada; they led on a few ignorant dupes until they got them wheTe they wanted them. At that point section 98 came into play and arrests were made. Surely the powers that be ought to hesitate to stoop to that sort of thing. Yet it was done, and maybe it is going on now to a greater extent. Perhaps the most radical revolutionary papers in Canada are being edited by agents of that type, who desire to prove the value of section 98, and to make connections with the groups in this comer of the house in an effort to gain ground for the argument that there is an association between the two.

The hon. member has mentioned a very notable and exceptionally well edited paper which is very far ahead of any paper which at the moment can be claimed in support of the Conservative party.
Then, another group who want to retain section 98 are those who are afraid. They may have personal cause for fear about which I do not know, or their fears may be purely pathological. But that some of them have such fears there can be little or no doubt; and fears have always in the past expressed themselves in obscurantism and persecution. The hon. member for East Algoma (Mr. Nicholson), who is not in his seat, is in my

2330	COMMONS
Criminal Code-Unlawful Associations
opinion one of those people dominated by fear. He is so afraid that a resolution passed by the synod of his own church seemed to disturb him greatly. I have before me an excerpt from a news item appearing in the Ottawa Journal of September 23, which reads as follows:
Nicholson, M.P. urges resolution toned down lest they be misquoted on communist platforms.
Toronto, Sept. 22.-Anglican Synod-A demand for condemnation of "capitalistic methods'' and of financial scheming which takes millions from the many, to put into the hands of the few, was made by the Very Rev. Archdeacon F. G. Scott of Quebec, at the general synod of the church of England to-day.
On motion of Canon A. P. Gower Rees of Montreal, the synod committed itself to the principle that "the nation is primarily responsible for the support of any citizen who, through no fault of his own, is deprived of his right to secure his own means of livelihood and the maintenance of his dependents."
Moving that the resolutions be referred to the special committee G. B. Nicholson, M.P. of East Algoma urged that they be toned down "lest they be misquoted on communist platforms all across the country."
When the hon. member is actually afraid of the resolution passed by the Anglican synod, one cannot wonder that he would literally quake with fear at the resolutions which come from this corner of the house.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INSPECTION OF CANNED SALMON STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR COMMITTEE

Yes, so far as I can learn

maintopic: SUPPLY-INSPECTION OF CANNED SALMON STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: He was afraid of being misquoted.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INSPECTION OF CANNED SALMON STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Well the fear of misquotation is not expressed in the report which I read, and I have never heard any such fears expressed by the hon. gentleman here. It was always the reality of his imaginings he was afraid of, not of being misquoted. Now it appears to me that he and a few others in this house are suffering from Russiaphobia, and being in that condition they seem to be entirely unconscious that they are following Russian methods themselves. The attitude of the government in retaining section 98 and in arresting and imprisoning people under that section is undoubtedly that of the czar. That is the course the czar followed prior to the revolution. No matter how intelligent a man was, if he opposed the czar he was clubbed or murdered or sent to Siberia under laws similar to this that we are opposing. So that 
while hon. members apposite charge us with being bolshevists, I feel very much prouder of that than if I were on- the other side following in the footsteps of the czar across the sands of political time. And that is what they are doing. I say I would far rather be charged in this house or anywhere else with being a follower of Lenin than of the czar, though I am a follower of neither. Supporters of section 98 are followers of the czar. He who practises what the czar practised is a follower of the czar. This section 98 if it had been drawn by the czar would not have been any more rigorous than it is. Its method, its spirit, the political philosophy behind it, are those that were characteristic of the czar and led to the revolution which hon. gentlemen so much deplore and fear will be repeated. Economic slavery and persecution were the seeds of communism. Whatever associations hon. gentlemen may try to establish between the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, for instance, and groups associated with it, and the communistic groups, whatever success they can make of that they are welcome to, but I repeat, I would much rather be associated with communism than with the group to which they belong, namely the czaristic group. Section 98 is certainly not British, it is certainly not Canadian, it is a weapon of prerevolutionary Russia, and I do not marvel that those who advocate it are afraid. They are certainly taking a course which would give them cause for fear if they only realized it.
There is a third type that seem to desire to retain this legislation, namely those who honestly believe that ideas can be and should be put down by force. Those of us who want to see section 98 repealed believe that the widest possible latitude should be given to all thought, and that thoughts, whoever may express them, should be allowed to be uttered unhampered. I would not go so far with action; I quite realize that a government that cannot retain power ceases to be a government, and if force is exercised against the government then the government has to exercise force to maintain itself. In other words, if any group in Canada made forcible attacks upon government or upon the institutions necessary, to law and order, then I do not doubt that the government should take action, but for the government to begin to take action by force before any action has been taken against it is undoubtedly persecution. Let the government wait until the action has been taken against it; then it is time enough for the government to act. I suppose most of us have noticed that those who, like this parliament for instance, do a lot of talk-

Criminal Code-Unlawful Associations
ing, never act very quickly if at all. Great Britain has recognized that for a long time. She permits liberty of speech; men and women can go into the halls and the public parks of Great Britain and say what they like, there is no restriction on words or ideas. And Great Britain has found that that is much safer than to try to repress utterance. Think of the absurdity, for instance, of a single communist or a handful of communists standing up and saying that they are going to upset the Canadian government by force! There they are, a few poorly fed, poorly clad and sometimes ignorant individuals, with no organization, no money, no guns, no arsenal, no munitions, no aeroplanes, they have nothing but their mouths and they stand up and threaten to attack by force the government of this country! A ridiculous thing, a joke. Those, as a rule, who thus threaten attack by force, do so because of the realization of their utter inability to carry out their threat. If they really were trying to upset the government by force they would not be talking so much about it. Let them talk. Let them say what they will, as long as they do not act. When they act, and if their action be subversive, I agree that the government must be firm, but the government has authority to take action under those circumstances without this action, which, on the other hand, provides opportunity for any government inspired by fear to persecute instead of punish. There is the point, I think the most powerful point in the whole argument against the repeal of this section. In that connection may I refer to a statement which I think was made by Macaulay? He says:
The true distinction (between punishment and persecution) is obvious. To punish a man because he has committed a crime, or is believed, though unjustly, to have committed a crime, is not persecution. To punish a man because we infer from the nature of some doctrine which he holds, or from the conduct of other persons who hold the same doctrines with him, that he will commit a crime is persecution; and is in every case foolish and wicked.
It appears to me, sir, that that is the whole point at issue in regard to the repeal of section 98. The government has all the authority it requires for the protection of the government and the state. But this section gives them the opportunity to persecute if they desire to do so. I do not say that they wilfully desire to persecute, but when men are as afraid as the hon. member for East Algoma (Mr. Nicholson) and find themselves with a weapon of this sort at hand, they use it. It has been used rather liberally in the past few months, and if it is not taken away no doubt S3719-1475
will be used in the future perhaps even more liberally. So I hope, Mr. Speaker, that all who believe in freedom of thought, who believe that every man should have the right to express his views when and where he desires, will support the repeal of section 98. Let those who are afraid, those who desire to use it for persecution, keep on their fateful course; history will deal with them just as it did with their predecessor the Czar of Russia. But for those who wish to retain British institutions and who wish to give freedom to thought- or shall we say those who wish to retain Canadian institutions, which are perhaps even higher-I say, let us wipe this legislation from the statute books and allow Canadians the right to express themselves on political and economic and social questions as they feel inclined.

maintopic: SUPPLY-INSPECTION OF CANNED SALMON STATEMENT OF MR. NEILL ON MOTION OF MR. GUTHRIE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words in support of this measure which is before the house. I was surprised-and I suppose being surprised arises from the fact that I am a new member, because I notice that the older members are not surprised at anything that happens in the house-I was surprised, sir, when I heard the attacks of hon. gentlemen opposite on this bill, especially when they endeavoured in some way to connect Canadian labour with soviet Russia. I am sure no hon. member seriously believes that any member on this side of the house believes in or would advocate force or is connected in any way with soviet Russia. So I say I was rather surprised and also disappointed when 1 heard the attacks on hon. members supporting this bill. I can say this much, Mr. Speaker, that the communists of this country utter more denunciatory remarks against the labour members in this house than they do against even the vested interests; they are more severe in their criticisms of those who stand up for labour.
I hope the views expressed by hon. members opposite who have spoken are not held generally, because if those fears spread I am afraid we are then in danger of losing our individual liberty. For that reason, therefore, I would be loath to see the present act retained on our statute books. Not long ago a prominent judge on the Pacific coast said that if ever there were a time when individual rights should be respected and preserved it was during this trying period through which we are passing. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) said only two prosecutions had been carried on under this section since it was passed in 1919. I feel sure, Mr. Speaker, that those who supported
2332	COMMONS
Criminal Code-Unlawful Associations
the measure in those days had some reason to believe that this provision was necessary then in order to prevent rebellion or revolution, but since that time only two prosecutions have been carried out. The fears held at that time have been proved groundless, and I am convinced that the fears some hold now are equally groundless. I do not think we are in danger of revolution if we remove this section from the criminal code. In time of peace there is no need for any such provision, because the whole nation is calm and can reason out all such matters that might affect the peace of the country, but conditions are entirely different at present. A wave of fear is likely to spread over the whole country, and no one can tell what may happen if a panic of fear should spread from one end of Canada to the other. It might not be very difficult to start a reign of suppression if the fears I have heard expressed by hon. gentlemen opposite should spread to any great degree.
Let me remind hon. members that Great Britain has not forgotten her magna charta of individual liberty; for many years she has carried on in the belief that there is more danger from bottled steam than from steam that is allowed to escape. So she has wisely adopted the policy of allowing any person to say almost anything so long as he does not go too far in regard to the king himself. He can say almost anything, however, with regard to the government. I have listened to speakers in Glasgow who had to be protected from those who wished to mob them for daring to say the government was evil. As I say, Great Britain has adopted the policy of permitting great freedom of speech in all public places; public speakers are protected by the law and are allowed to say what they wish. If you do not care to listen or do not agree with what they are saying it is your privilege to walk on and pay no attention to them. It might be well, Mr. Speaker, if hon. members who could afford it took the opportunity to visit that great country. We have heard a great deal about the Anglo-Saxon spirit, and we pretend to follow the lead of Great Britain in a great many things. Let us follow her lead in this case. For years the socialists and communists have been preaching their doctrines in that country but Britain is still as sane as ever. At the last election some people thought Great Britain would swing to socialism, but a national government was formed. Even Stalin, after the results of the last election were known, said that Great Britain was impossible. He believed that after socialistic doctrines had been preached there for so long,
[Mr. Reid.l
with unemployment prevalent and the depression and distress continuing, revolution was at hand and that after the election the socialist party would take charge of the country. That did not happen, however, due to the good sense and foresight of the British nation, which had allowed absolute freedom of speech.
I say, Mr. Speaker, that you can never keep down any movement by repression or force.
I remember very well that even Kier Hardie, the great labour leader, preached the red flag and taught socialist hymns in the Sunday schools in my younger days. Those hymns have been repeated in this country, and many members opposite seem greatly exercised in connection with them. I do not advocate immunity for those who would take charge of the government of this country by violence and bloodshed, but I do not think the removal of this section of the criminal code will bring about any such revolution in this country. I heard the Minister of Justice mention the long list of foreigners who were connected with the communist movement. I hope he does not make the mistake I made two years ago. There was a communist riot in the city of Vancouver, and I happened to say to the mayor of that city, "I suppose most of the leaders of these men are foreigners?" He said, "You are darned right they are foreigners; the head man is a Scotchman." Scotchmen are noted however for their great love of liberty, but I would not like them to be classed as foreigners.
There is a striking difference between the attitude taken by hon. gentlemen opposite and that taken by those on this side of the house; there is really a clear line of demarcation. The Liberal party and those in this corner of the house-and this is not another move to the left_have been in favour of individual liberty and took that attitude even when this measure was introduced in 1919. Those on the government benches fear that some great catastrophe will result if this amendment is carried. But the repeal of this provision is not asked for by labour only. I have had communications from many farm organizations asking me to do everything in my power to bring about the repeal of this section if the opportunity should arise. I greatly fear, Mr. Speaker, that if a wave of panic should sweep across the country the citizens of Canada may suffer greatly; they may be subjected to many injustices on suspicion only. We are told that the courts give a man a fair trial. That may be so, but in days of panic it is possible that the courts might become a little panicky also. History has proved that repression and force never stamped out a movement such as this. We know that to be the case in connection with

Criminal Code-Unlawful Associations
religion. In the early days endeavours were made to repress individual liberty in connection with religion, but it was found that this end was not accomplished. I might say to the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine) that the greater the repression, the better for any new movement. History has demonstrated this to be the fact.
I would ask hon. members opposite to use their calm judgment; if this panic spreads among the members of the house no one knows what may happen and what numbers of people may suffer. Repression is repulsive to the Anglo-Saxon. The way to keep communism from our country is to endeavour to work out some measures which will benefit the masses of the people, and if we can do that we need have no fear of communism or of a revolution, in my opinion. The people cannot be blamed if they gather in groups and talk and scheme about a new social order. Surely it is their right to do so, especially when we have hundreds of thousands of unemployed, not only in this country but in every other country in the world. Surely, when they have lost their all and have become charges on the state, they have a right to endeavour to take steps to better their conditions and talk about a new social order. Sometimes I think the city of Ottawa is as far removed from the rest of Canada in her knowledge of actual conditions as Siberia is removed from the rest of Russia. I do not think you can properly get the viewpoint of the rest of Canada from this city.
For all these reasons, and many others, Mr. Speaker, I shall take great pleasure in voting for this measure to repeal section 98.

speechtext:
I did not intend at first to take part in the debate, but as I listened to the arguments of the ex-Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) I thought I should say a few words. I heard the hon. gentleman speak in favour of the repeal of section 98, and one of the arguments he used was that the other clauses in the criminal code are quite sufficient to deal with the situation. This is the legal opinion of a high personage whom I respect, but it is not my opinion. I do not agree with the hon. member for Quebec East when he says that section 98 is legislation that should be repealed; on the contrary I think it is the only legislation which adequately meets the case against communism. In my opinion, and it is only a personal opinion, sections 87, 89, 130 to 136 of the code do not sufficiently cover communism, and if the hon. member for Quebec East is right, which I deny, then section 98 is only a mere repetition. If it is only a repetition why oppose it so strongly?
There is a very simple way of nullifying the purport of section 98 and that is for every man in this country to abide by the law and not to try to soviet or revolutionize or to overthrow the social order by force, violence or physical injury to persons or property. Section 98 does not affect the ordinary trade and labour organizations or unions; they have nothing to fear from that section. The law abiding citizen has no reason to be apprehensive of section 98, and the section is by no means an attack on the right of free speech. Any citizen may advocate the most radical changes and criticize in the most emphatic language our institutions and laws; it is only when force, violence or physical injury to person or property is used or threatened to be used that the section applies.
An additional argument advanced by the hon. member for Quebec East is this. He said that such legislation is arbitrary and contrary to the ordinary rules of British justice and British procedure. I presume my hon. friend meant en resume that it was opposed to liberalism. I wonder what liberalism he meant. Is it his own liberalism or the liberalism practised by his party in the province of Quebec? A study of the Quebec Alcoholic Liquor Act will show that by that act are abolished all the writs of prerogative. By section 139 no writ of quo warranto, of injunction or of certiorari may be granted; no writ of mandamus and no writ of prohibition may be issued. Even the sacred rights of habeas corpus are abrogated by section 130 of the Quebec Alcoholic Liquor Act. Another Quebec law, the Alcoholic Liquor Possession and Transportation Act, also abolishes all these writs of prerogative, including even the habeas corpus; whereas section 98 of our criminal code does not abolish the habeas corpus although it is for a higher purpose than the Quebec liquor acts, its object being the maintenance of peace, order and good government.
It is very amusing to hear our friends advocating the principles of liberalism. On the one hand we see the ex-Minister of Justice advocating the repeal of section 98, and on the other hand we find his friends in Quebec abolishing the writs of prerogative and habeas corpus. It reminds me of what I heard one day in Quebec; it was on the 14th of January 1933. The Liberals gave a big demonstration to their chief, the leader of the opposition, at

Criminal Code-Unlawful Associations
a huge banquet. We heard the Hon. Mr. Tas-chereau saying that maybe democracy had gone too far and that we should go back, and immediately afterwards we heard the hon. member for Quebec East declaring that on the contrary we should go forward. At that meeting we had the great privilege of listening by radio to the views of these gentlemen. It was a love feast of Liberal adherents and we had the privilege of listening to the most interesting contradictory meeting one could attend.
I admit that this is exceptional legislation. The Minister of Justice admitted the other day that there had been times in the past when he looked upon the repeal of this section as a matter of indifference; he even added that on one oocasion he stated that this particular section had perhaps survived its usefulness and that there was no further necessity for it. But, added my hon. colleague, at that time there was no communist agitation in this country such as prevails to-day. May I add that this communist agitation is spreading and gaining ground all over Canada. We think therefore that the only legislation which adequately meets the situation is this section 98; we look upon it as a rampart against communism.
I will not quote at length some of the passages of such literature as is actually circulated throughout this country; I should be afraid of promoting its propaganda. I do say however that the Minister of Justice was quite correct when he stated that the literature circulated is most scandalous, most seditious and in many cases blasphemous and obscene.
Section 98 was inserted in 1919 and up to 1926 there was mo move om the part of my hon. friends, who were then in power, towards the repeal of that provision. Then came the elections of 1925 and both parties were returned with almost equal strength. Then followed the famous letter written by my hon. friends of the Labour party, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) and the hon. member for Vancouver asking the then Prime Minister the price to be paid if he wanted the support of the two members.

Let us for the moment examine section 98. The first paragraph refers to any association, and so forth, that advocates force, violence or physical injury. No hon. member will be a party to advocating violence or physical injury to any person or property. But what is the meaning of the word "force"? If the words "physical injury" are used, why put in "force"? Is this not a case of moral force?
A recent occurrence in Toronto shows how extremely ridiculous a situation may be rendered. A couple of young lads from the Jarvis collegiate were distributing cards to their co-students to attend a meeting of the high school boys to discuss social and economic problems. The principal of the school, after looking at the cards, was rather put out and called in a policeman. The policeman thoroughly examined the boys and ascertained that they were calling a meeting of the high school students in a certain hall for the purpose of discussing social and economic problems. But through some workings of the police, the owner of the hall was frightened out of allowing its use to those boys, with the consequence that the meeting was cancelled. Just imagine! High school boys gathered together for the purpose of discussing our social and economic problems, and the power of the police force used against them with the result that they are unable to meet and discuss those problems!
